properties.title: Mexico at independence (1821)
properties.label: Mexico 1821
properties.description: The territory claimed by independent Mexico in 1821: the former Viceroyalty of New Spain north of Central America, bounded in the north by the line Spain had agreed with the United States in 1819. Much of the north (Texas, New Mexico, the Californias) was thinly settled, and large areas were actually controlled by independent Comanche, Apache, Navajo and other nations rather than by the Mexican state.
properties.note: Northern edge follows the Adams–Onís line; southern edge uses the modern Mexico–Guatemala and Mexico–Belize borders, which were only fixed by treaties of 1882 and 1893, so it includes Chiapas, which in 1821 still belonged to the Kingdom of Guatemala (it adhered to the Plan of Iguala in 1821, was annexed in January 1822 and confirmed its union with Mexico in 1824; Soconusco stayed disputed until 1842). Coasts are modern.

sources.citation: Treaty of Amity, Settlement, and Limits between the United States and Spain (Adams–Onís Treaty), signed 22 Feb 1819, art. III. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Adams–Onís Treaty line (1819; in force 1821)
properties.label: Adams–Onís line 1819
properties.description: Spain and the United States agreed this boundary in 1819 (ratifications exchanged February 1821), and Mexico inherited it, confirming it with the US in the Treaty of Limits of 1828 (ratified 1832). It runs up the Sabine River to 32°N, north to the Red River, up the Red River to 100°W, north to the Arkansas, up the Arkansas to its source, north to 42°N and west along that parallel to the Pacific.
properties.note: Built from the treaty text: the Sabine and Red River sections follow the modern Texas border, the Arkansas follows Natural Earth river data, and the treaty's "source of the Arkansas … in latitude 42" is drawn as a meridian from the actual source to 42°N, as the treaty's contingency clause specifies (this segment was never surveyed). Strictly the line follows the west bank of the Sabine and the south banks of the Red and Arkansas. The treaty's 100th meridian was taken from the Melish map and was later surveyed differently.

sources.citation: Treaty of Amity, Settlement, and Limits between the United States and Spain (Adams–Onís Treaty), signed 22 Feb 1819, art. III. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).

properties.title: Central America in the Mexican Empire (1822–1823)
properties.label: Central America
properties.description: The provinces of the former Kingdom of Guatemala voted to join Iturbide's Mexican Empire in January 1822, and Mexican troops under Vicente Filísola occupied El Salvador to enforce it. After Iturbide fell, a Central American congress declared independence from Mexico on 1 July 1823, creating the United Provinces of Central America. Chiapas briefly declared itself free and in 1824 opted for Mexico, while Soconusco remained disputed until Santa Anna annexed it in 1842.
properties.note: Drawn with the modern borders of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica; colonial internal boundaries and the British settlements in Belize and on the Mosquito Coast are not represented.

sources.citation: Ralph Lee Woodward Jr., Central America: A Nation Divided, 3rd ed. (Oxford University Press, 1999).
Mario Vázquez Olivera, El Imperio mexicano y el Reino de Guatemala: proyecto político y campaña militar, 1821–1823 (Fondo de Cultura Económica, 2009).
Timothy E. Anna, The Mexican Empire of Iturbide (University of Nebraska Press, 1990).

properties.title: Texas as claimed by the Republic (1836)
properties.label: Texas claim 1836
properties.description: The Texas Congress's boundary act of December 1836 claimed everything east and north of the Rio Grande from its mouth to its source, then north to 42°N, far beyond the area Texas controlled. Mexico refused to recognise the Republic (its belated 1845 offer of recognition on condition that Texas reject annexation came too late). The US annexed Texas in 1845 "subject to the adjustment" of boundary questions, but President Polk adopted the Rio Grande claim, and the dispute over the land between the Nueces and the Rio Grande became the trigger of war. In the Compromise of 1850 Texas gave up its claim north of 36°30′ and west of 103°W in return for $10 million, keeping only the land below 32°N west of 103°W around El Paso.
properties.note: Follows the 1836 act's description; the upper Rio Grande uses Natural Earth river data.

sources.citation: Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Boundaries".
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).

properties.title: The Nueces Strip (disputed 1836–1848)
properties.label: Nueces Strip
properties.description: Under Spain and Mexico the province of Texas ended at the Nueces River; Texas, and then the United States, claimed to the Rio Grande. In 1846 President Polk ordered Zachary Taylor into this strip, and the clash there in April gave Polk his claim that Mexico had "shed American blood upon the American soil".
properties.note: The strip is closed in the west by a schematic line from the Nueces headwaters to the Rio Grande.

sources.citation: Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Nueces River".
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).

properties.title: Mexican Cession (1848)
properties.label: Mexican Cession 1848
properties.description: By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexico ceded Alta California and New Mexico for $15 million and the assumption of claims, giving up about half of its claimed territory (counting Texas). Gold had been found in California nine days before the treaty was signed. Mexican residents who stayed were promised US citizenship and protection of their property.
properties.note: Bounded by 42°N, the Texas claim, and the 1848 line. Land east of the upper Rio Grande claimed by Texas is shown with the Texas claim, following the usual convention.

sources.citation: Treaty of Peace, Friendship, Limits, and Settlement (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo), signed 2 Feb 1848, art. V. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paula Rebert, La Gran Línea: Mapping the United States–Mexico Boundary, 1849–1857 (University of Texas Press, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo boundary (1848)
properties.label: Guadalupe Hidalgo line 1848
properties.description: Article V ran the border up the Rio Grande "to the point where it strikes the southern boundary of New Mexico", west along that boundary, north to the Gila, down the Gila to the Colorado, and then in a straight line to the Pacific one marine league south of San Diego Bay. Because the treaty map (Disturnell, 1847) misplaced El Paso and the Rio Grande, the location of New Mexico's southern boundary was disputed until the Gadsden Treaty replaced it.
properties.note: The New Mexico section is drawn at 32°22′N for three degrees of longitude west of the Rio Grande and then north to the Gila, as in the Bartlett–García Conde compromise negotiated in 1850–51 (the US never implemented it; in 1852 Congress barred funds for surveying it). The Rio Grande follows the modern border and Natural Earth river data; the river has since shifted.

sources.citation: Treaty of Peace, Friendship, Limits, and Settlement (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo), signed 2 Feb 1848, art. V. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
Paula Rebert, La Gran Línea: Mapping the United States–Mexico Boundary, 1849–1857 (University of Texas Press, 2001).
International Boundary and Water Commission, United States and Mexico, "History of the International Boundary".

properties.title: Gadsden Purchase (La Mesilla) 1853–1854
properties.label: Gadsden Purchase
properties.description: Santa Anna's last government sold the Mesilla Valley and the land south of the Gila to the United States for $10 million, settling the boundary dispute and giving the US a practical southern railroad route to California. The sale was deeply unpopular in Mexico and helped bring down Santa Anna in the Revolution of Ayutla.
properties.note: Southern edge follows the treaty's surveyed line (now the international border); the northern edge inherits the uncertainty of the 1848 line.

sources.citation: Gadsden Purchase Treaty (Treaty of La Mesilla), signed 30 Dec 1853, art. I as amended by the US Senate. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
Paula Rebert, La Gran Línea: Mapping the United States–Mexico Boundary, 1849–1857 (University of Texas Press, 2001).
Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Gadsden Treaty boundary (1853)
properties.label: Gadsden line 1853
properties.description: The treaty boundary, surveyed in 1855: from the Rio Grande at 31°47′N due west 100 miles, south to 31°20′N, west along that parallel to the 111th meridian, then in a straight line to the Colorado River twenty miles below its junction with the Gila, and up the Colorado. It is the present border of New Mexico and Arizona with Chihuahua and Sonora, and along the Colorado between Arizona and Baja California.

sources.citation: Gadsden Purchase Treaty (Treaty of La Mesilla), signed 30 Dec 1853, art. I as amended by the US Senate. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
International Boundary and Water Commission, United States and Mexico, "History of the International Boundary".
Paula Rebert, La Gran Línea: Mapping the United States–Mexico Boundary, 1849–1857 (University of Texas Press, 2001).

properties.title: Iturbide's empire
properties.label: Iturbide crowned
properties.description: Agustín de Iturbide, the royalist officer who had negotiated independence, was proclaimed emperor in May 1822 and crowned in the cathedral of Mexico City on 21 July. He dissolved Congress, ran out of money, and was overthrown by a revolt of provincial garrisons under the Plan of Casa Mata; he abdicated in March 1823.

sources.citation: Timothy E. Anna, The Mexican Empire of Iturbide (University of Nebraska Press, 1990).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Santa Anna's revolt at Veracruz and the Plan of Casa Mata
properties.label: Plan of Casa Mata
properties.description: In December 1822 Antonio López de Santa Anna rose at Veracruz against Iturbide, who had dissolved Congress. The imperial army sent to besiege the port under José Antonio Echávarri came to terms with the rebels instead, and on 1 February 1823 proclaimed the Plan of Casa Mata, named after a powder magazine outside the city, calling for a new congress and leaving the provinces to govern themselves through their deputations. The provincial garrisons adhered one after another and Iturbide abdicated on 19 March 1823. Gillingham treats Iguala and Casa Mata as the models of the pronunciamiento, the choreographed military revolt that made and unmade governments for the next half-century.
properties.note: Marked in Veracruz; the Casa Mata magazine stood outside the old city walls and is not located. Dated from the December revolt to the abdication.

sources.citation: Nettie Lee Benson, "The Plan of Casa Mata," Hispanic American Historical Review 25, no. 1 (1945): 45–56.
Timothy E. Anna, The Mexican Empire of Iturbide (University of Nebraska Press, 1990).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Central America separates from Mexico
properties.label: Central America separates
properties.description: A National Constituent Assembly meeting in Guatemala City declared the provinces of Central America independent of Mexico and of any other power. Mexico accepted the separation, but Chiapas chose to remain Mexican.

sources.citation: Ralph Lee Woodward Jr., Central America: A Nation Divided, 3rd ed. (Oxford University Press, 1999).
Mario Vázquez Olivera, El Imperio mexicano y el Reino de Guatemala: proyecto político y campaña militar, 1821–1823 (Fondo de Cultura Económica, 2009).

properties.title: Federal Constitution of 1824
properties.label: Constitution of 1824
properties.description: Mexico's first constitution created a federal republic of 19 states and 4 territories, with Catholicism as the sole permitted religion. The tension between federalists, who wanted strong states, and centralists, who wanted a strong capital, shaped the next three decades and much of the territorial loss.
properties.note: Marked at the former church of San Pedro y San Pablo, where the Constituent Congress met (now the Museo de las Constituciones). Gillingham (ch. 9) counts nineteen states, five territories and a federal district; the constitution itself named four territories and left Tlaxcala's status to a later law, and Tlaxcala (as a territory) and the Federal District were both created by decrees of November 1824.
properties.modern_place: Museo de las Constituciones, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Josefina Zoraida Vázquez, "Los primeros tropiezos", in Historia general de México, versión 2000 (El Colegio de México, 2000).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Chiapas joins Mexico
properties.label: Chiapas joins Mexico
properties.description: After the Central American separation, Chiapas, formerly part of the Kingdom of Guatemala, held a consultation and declared for union with Mexico. Soconusco, on the Pacific coast, stayed disputed between Mexico and Guatemala until Mexico occupied it in 1842; Guatemala renounced it in the treaty of 1882.
properties.note: Marked at Ciudad Real, today San Cristóbal de las Casas, then the provincial capital.
properties.modern_place: San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Mario Vázquez Olivera, El Imperio mexicano y el Reino de Guatemala: proyecto político y campaña militar, 1821–1823 (Fondo de Cultura Económica, 2009).

properties.title: Iturbide shot at Padilla
properties.label: Iturbide shot
properties.description: After a year in exile in Italy and England, Iturbide sailed back to Mexico, apparently unaware that Congress had outlawed him and decreed his death if he set foot in the country. He landed at Soto la Marina on 14 July 1824, was recognised and arrested, and was taken to Padilla, where the Tamaulipas state congress was sitting. The congress refused to hear him and had him shot the same day it confirmed the sentence, 19 July.
properties.note: Marked at modern Padilla. The old Villa de Padilla, where he was shot, was flooded by the Vicente Guerrero reservoir in 1970–71 and lies under the water a short distance away.

sources.citation: Timothy E. Anna, The Mexican Empire of Iturbide (University of Nebraska Press, 1990).
"Bajo millones de metros cúbicos de agua yace el pueblo donde fusilaron a Agustín de Iturbide," Milenio.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Spanish garrison holds San Juan de Ulúa (1821–1825)
properties.label: Ulúa held by Spain
properties.description: Spain did not accept the Treaty of Córdoba, and in October 1821 the last Spanish troops under Brigadier José Dávila withdrew to the island fortress of San Juan de Ulúa, whose guns commanded the harbour of Veracruz. In September 1823 the garrison began a bombardment of the town that lasted three months and drove out its inhabitants, and shipping was diverted to other ports such as Tampico. Mexico bought warships with its London loans, and in 1825 a blockade under Pedro Sáinz de Baranda kept relief from Cuba away until the last few dozen sick and starving defenders capitulated in November.
properties.note: The capitulation is dated 17 or 18 November 1825 and the handover 23 November, the date shown as the end. The point is nudged a little away from the Pastry War point at the same fortress.
properties.modern_place: San Juan de Ulúa, Veracruz, Mexico

sources.citation: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia, "Rememoran rendición española en San Juan de Ulúa, en 1825," Boletín no. 588, 6 November 2025.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Yaqui rising under Juan Banderas (1825–1833)
properties.label: Juan Banderas
properties.description: When soldiers sent to collect taxes were driven out of the Yaqui pueblos, Juan Ignacio Jusacamea, called Banderas from the banner he carried and said had belonged to Moctezuma, raised the Yaquis, Mayos and their neighbours against the Sonoran authorities, aiming at an Indian confederation that would return the land to its original owners. Between risings he made peace with the state, which Gillingham says secured the Yaquis the river valley, while raiding haciendas and gathering arms. He rose again at the end of 1832, was defeated and captured, and was shot at Arizpe on 23 January 1833.
properties.note: Marked at Ráhum, one of the Yaqui river pueblos, which Dedrick identifies as the meeting place of the movement; the fighting ranged over southern Sonora, and Banderas was executed at Arizpe, far to the north.

sources.citation: John M. Dedrick, "Las cartas en yaqui de Juan 'Bandera'," Tlalocan 10 (1985).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Spanish reconquest attempt defeated at Tampico
properties.label: Tampico 1829
properties.description: Spain, which did not recognise Mexican independence until 1836, landed an expedition from Cuba under Isidro Barradas (Gillingham gives 3,500 men) on the coast south of Tampico, and it occupied the town in August 1829. Weakened by yellow fever and besieged by forces under Santa Anna and Manuel de Mier y Terán, it surrendered, making Santa Anna a national hero.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.note: Marked at Tampico, which the expedition occupied; the siege and surrender took place around the town. Gillingham (ch. 10) dates Santa Anna's attack on the Spanish stockade at the mouth of the Pánuco to 7 September; the date shown is the surrender, which followed the assault of the night of 10–11 September.

properties.title: Vicente Guerrero shot at Cuilapan
properties.label: Guerrero shot
properties.description: Guerrero, the insurgent chief of the south and an Afro-Mexican mule driver from Tixtla, became president in 1829 after a disputed election and a revolt in the capital; his government abolished slavery and beat off the Spanish landing at Tampico, but his vice-president Anastasio Bustamante overthrew him in December 1829. While Guerrero fought on in the south, the Genoese captain Francisco Picaluga lured him aboard his ship at Acapulco on 14 January 1831 and handed him over. He was court-martialled in Oaxaca and shot at Cuilapan on 14 February. Gillingham calls him the first Black president in North American history.
properties.note: Marked at the former Dominican convent of Cuilapan, where he was held and shot.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, "Fusilamiento de Vicente Guerrero, insurgente que consumó la independencia; primer presidente afromexicano. 14 de febrero de 1831."
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Santa Anna crushes the Zacatecas militia
properties.label: Zacatecas 1835
properties.description: As Congress moved toward a centralist system, the state of Zacatecas, with the country's strongest civic militia, refused to disband it. Santa Anna defeated the militia at Guadalupe and let his troops sack Zacatecas. The suppression of federalism helped push Texas, and later Yucatán, toward secession.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).
Josefina Zoraida Vázquez, "Los primeros tropiezos", in Historia general de México, versión 2000 (El Colegio de México, 2000).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Battle of Gonzales
properties.label: Gonzales
properties.description: Mexican troops sent to recover a small cannon from the Anglo-American settlers of Gonzales were driven off ("come and take it"), the first fighting of the Texas Revolution. Estimates vary, but by 1835 Anglo-American settlers and the people they enslaved far outnumbered Texas's few thousand Tejanos.
properties.note: The skirmish took place a few miles west of Gonzales, near present-day Cost.

sources.citation: Stephen L. Hardin, Texian Iliad: A Military History of the Texas Revolution, 1835–1836 (University of Texas Press, 1994).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Gonzales, Battle of".

properties.title: Siege and battle of the Alamo
properties.label: Alamo
properties.description: Santa Anna's army besieged the former mission of San Antonio de Valero at Béxar and stormed it on 6 March, killing nearly all of its defenders (189 are on the official list; research suggests up to about 257). The Texas convention had declared independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos four days earlier.

sources.citation: Stephen L. Hardin, Texian Iliad: A Military History of the Texas Revolution, 1835–1836 (University of Texas Press, 1994).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Alamo, Battle of the".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Goliad massacre
properties.label: Goliad
properties.description: After surrendering at the battle of Coleto, about 340 prisoners, most of them James Fannin's command, were executed at Presidio La Bahía on Palm Sunday on Santa Anna's orders, under a decree treating armed foreigners as pirates. With the Alamo, it became a rallying cry for the Texan army.

sources.citation: Stephen L. Hardin, Texian Iliad: A Military History of the Texas Revolution, 1835–1836 (University of Texas Press, 1994).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Goliad Massacre".

properties.title: Battle of San Jacinto
properties.label: San Jacinto
properties.description: Sam Houston's army surprised Santa Anna's camp near the junction of Buffalo Bayou and the San Jacinto River and routed it in under twenty minutes. Santa Anna was captured the next day.
properties.modern_place: San Jacinto Battleground State Historic Site

sources.citation: Stephen L. Hardin, Texian Iliad: A Military History of the Texas Revolution, 1835–1836 (University of Texas Press, 1994).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "San Jacinto, Battle of".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Treaties of Velasco
properties.label: Velasco
properties.description: As a prisoner, Santa Anna signed public and secret agreements to withdraw Mexican troops beyond the Rio Grande and work for recognition of Texas. On 20 May the government in Mexico City declared void all acts Santa Anna performed as a captive, and Mexico continued to regard Texas as a rebel province.
properties.note: Velasco, at the mouth of the Brazos, no longer exists; its site is within modern Surfside Beach and Freeport.

sources.citation: Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Treaties of Velasco".
Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).

properties.title: United States annexes Texas
properties.label: Annexation of Texas
properties.description: After a joint resolution of Congress in March 1845 and acceptance by a Texas convention at Austin in July, Texas was admitted to the Union on 29 December 1845. Mexico had warned that annexation would mean war and broke off diplomatic relations.
properties.note: Marked at Austin, the capital of the Republic and site of the annexation convention.

sources.citation: Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Annexation".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Santa Fe Trail
properties.label: Santa Fe Trail
properties.description: Spain had kept New Mexico closed to foreign trade; independent Mexico opened it, and in 1821 William Becknell took goods from Missouri to Santa Fe. The trail turned New Mexico's commerce toward the United States rather than Chihuahua and Mexico City, and in 1846 Kearny's army marched west along it. It remained the main route to New Mexico until the railroad arrived in 1879–80.
properties.note: Shows the Cimarron route via Franklin, Independence, Council Grove, the Arkansas crossing near Cimarron (Kansas), Wagon Mound and Las Vegas; the Mountain route via Bent's Fort is followed by Kearny's march. The section across the Cimarron desert is schematic.

sources.citation: Josiah Gregg, Commerce of the Prairies (New York, 1844).
US National Park Service, Santa Fe National Historic Trail.
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).

properties.title: Russian settlement at Fort Ross (1812–1841)
properties.label: Fort Ross
properties.description: The Russian-American Company, based at Sitka in Alaska, founded Fort Ross on the coast north of San Francisco Bay in 1812, near its anchorage at Bodega, as a base for hunting sea otters and growing food for its Alaskan posts. Neither Spain nor Mexico could remove the stockaded, cannon-armed post, which outlasted Spanish rule by twenty years. The company sold it to John Sutter in December 1841, after the otters had been hunted out; Gillingham uses it to show how exposed Mexico's Pacific north was to rival empires.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 10) dates the colony 1811–1839; California State Parks gives 1812–1841, and the bill of sale to Sutter is dated 20 December 1841. The feature begins before the era because the post outlived Spanish rule.

sources.citation: California Department of Parks and Recreation, "Fort Ross State Historic Park."
Fort Ross Conservancy, "Fort Ross Bill of Sale."
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Pastry War: French bombardment of San Juan de Ulúa
properties.label: Pastry War
properties.description: France blockaded Mexican ports from April 1838 to press claims by French nationals (one a pastry cook, hence the name). On 27 November its squadron bombarded San Juan de Ulúa, which surrendered; in a fight in Veracruz on 5 December Santa Anna lost his leg and regained his popularity. Mexico agreed to pay 600,000 pesos in March 1839.

sources.citation: Nancy Nichols Barker, The French Experience in Mexico, 1821–1861: A History of Constant Misunderstanding (University of North Carolina Press, 1979).
Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Yucatán breaks away
properties.label: Republic of Yucatán
properties.description: Rejecting centralism and the trade restrictions that came with it, Yucatán's elite declared the peninsula independent in 1841, hired the Texan navy to guard its coast, fought off a Mexican invasion in 1842–43 and stayed neutral in the US war. Facing defeat in the Caste War, it rejoined Mexico in 1848 in exchange for military aid.
properties.note: Marked at Mérida. The separation went through several declarations and reunions; only the overall span is given.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Terry Rugeley, Yucatán's Maya Peasantry and the Origins of the Caste War (University of Texas Press, 1996).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 9.

properties.title: Caste War begins at Tepich
properties.label: Tepich
properties.description: After the execution of the Maya leader Manuel Antonio Ay, Cecilio Chi attacked the town of Tepich, beginning the Caste War. The rising grew out of the spread of sugar estates onto Maya lands, taxation, and the arming of Maya soldiers in the region's factional wars.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Terry Rugeley, Yucatán's Maya Peasantry and the Origins of the Caste War (University of Texas Press, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Maya forces take Valladolid
properties.label: Valladolid 1848
properties.description: At the height of the war in spring 1848 the rebels captured Valladolid, one of the peninsula's principal cities, and advanced to within a short distance of Mérida and Campeche before withdrawing at planting time. Yucatán's government offered sovereignty to Spain, Britain and the United States in return for help before turning back to Mexico.
properties.note: The city was evacuated in March 1848; sources give slightly different days.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Terry Rugeley, Yucatán's Maya Peasantry and the Origins of the Caste War (University of Texas Press, 1996).

properties.title: Chan Santa Cruz and the Speaking Cross
properties.label: Chan Santa Cruz
properties.description: Driven back into the forests of the east, rebel Maya gathered around a cross said to speak at a cenote (Gillingham: the Talking Cross), and Chan Santa Cruz became the capital of an independent Maya polity (the Cruzob) that traded arms through British Honduras. Mexican federal troops occupied it only in 1901; the town is now Felipe Carrillo Puerto.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Territory of the rebel Maya (c. 1850s–1901)
properties.label: Rebel Maya territory
properties.description: After 1849 the war settled into a long frontier: the Cruzob Maya held the forests of the eastern peninsula from around Tulum to Bacalar (retaken by them in 1858), while the state of Yucatán held the northwest. Other Maya groups to the south (the "pacíficos") made separate peace with Mexico.
properties.note: The frontier moved repeatedly and was never surveyed; this outline only indicates the core area.

sources.citation: Nelson A. Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán, rev. ed. (Stanford University Press, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Taylor's campaign in the northeast
properties.label: Taylor 1846–47
properties.description: Zachary Taylor's army moved from Corpus Christi to the Rio Grande opposite Matamoros in March 1846. After winning at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma it crossed the river, moved up to Camargo, and marched overland via Cerralvo to Monterrey and Saltillo, where it held off Santa Anna's army at Buena Vista in February 1847.
properties.note: Main stops only. The march between the Rio Grande and Point Isabel before the May battles is omitted. Gillingham (ch. 10) dates the occupation of the disputed strip to 13 January 1846, the day Polk ordered Taylor to the Rio Grande; the army left Corpus Christi on 8 March.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Thornton Affair
properties.label: Thornton Affair
properties.description: Mexican cavalry under Anastasio Torrejón ambushed a US patrol under Captain Seth Thornton on the north bank of the Rio Grande upriver from Matamoros. Polk used the clash to ask Congress for war, which it declared on 13 May 1846.
properties.note: Fought at Rancho de Carricitos, about 28 river miles above Fort Texas; the point follows the National Park Service's location but the exact site is uncertain. NPS gives 24 April; most sources give 25 April. Gillingham (ch. 10) gives 12 May for the declaration of war, the day the Senate passed it; Polk signed it on the 13th.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
US National Park Service, Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of Palo Alto
properties.label: Palo Alto
properties.description: The first major battle of the war, fought on the coastal prairie north of Matamoros. US light artillery broke up the attacks of Mariano Arista's larger army.
properties.modern_place: Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
US National Park Service, Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park.

properties.title: Battle of Resaca de la Palma
properties.label: Resaca de la Palma
properties.description: The day after Palo Alto, Taylor attacked Arista's army in a dry riverbed (resaca) and routed it; many Mexican soldiers drowned recrossing the Rio Grande. Taylor occupied Matamoros on 18 May.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
US National Park Service, Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park.

properties.title: Battle of Monterrey
properties.label: Monterrey
properties.description: Taylor attacked the fortified city of Monterrey, the key to the northeast, and took it after street fighting. He granted the garrison an eight-week armistice, which Polk repudiated.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 10) gives 20–23 September.

properties.title: Battle of Buena Vista (La Angostura)
properties.label: Buena Vista
properties.description: Santa Anna marched an army across the desert from San Luis Potosí and attacked Taylor's smaller force at the pass of La Angostura south of Saltillo. After two days of heavy fighting the Mexican army withdrew, having lost many men on the march. It was the last major battle in the northeast.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Will Fowler, Santa Anna of Mexico (University of Nebraska Press, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Kearny and the Army of the West
properties.label: Kearny 1846
properties.description: Stephen Watts Kearny led the Army of the West from Fort Leavenworth along the Santa Fe Trail (via Bent's Fort and Raton Pass) and occupied Santa Fe without a fight. With about 100 dragoons he then went down the Rio Grande, across to the Gila, and down the Gila and across the Colorado Desert to California, where he was badly mauled at San Pasqual before reaching San Diego.
properties.note: The crossing from the Rio Grande to the Gila and the desert stretch are approximate. The army left Fort Leavenworth in detachments in late June 1846; sources give different days for Kearny's own departure.

sources.citation: Dwight L. Clarke, Stephen Watts Kearny: Soldier of the West (University of Oklahoma Press, 1961).
K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
US National Park Service, Santa Fe National Historic Trail.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Kearny occupies Santa Fe
properties.label: Santa Fe 1846
properties.description: Governor Manuel Armijo abandoned his defensive position at Apache Canyon, and Kearny raised the US flag in Santa Fe's plaza without fighting. He proclaimed New Mexico part of the United States and issued a legal code before leaving for California.

sources.citation: Dwight L. Clarke, Stephen Watts Kearny: Soldier of the West (University of Oklahoma Press, 1961).
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).
K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Taos Revolt
properties.label: Taos Revolt
properties.description: Nuevomexicanos and Taos Pueblo men rose against the US occupation, killing the appointed governor Charles Bent at Taos and others elsewhere. US troops under Sterling Price crushed the revolt at Taos Pueblo in early February and hanged a number of leaders.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).

properties.title: Bear Flag Revolt
properties.label: Bear Flag Revolt
properties.description: American settlers, encouraged by the presence of John C. Frémont's survey party, seized the Mexican post at Sonoma, took Mariano Vallejo prisoner, and proclaimed a "California Republic" before news of the war arrived.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).

properties.title: US Navy seizes Monterey
properties.label: Monterey 1846
properties.description: Commodore John D. Sloat landed sailors and marines at Monterey, the capital of Alta California, and proclaimed the annexation of California. Resistance by Californios in the south in late 1846 drove US forces out of Los Angeles for several months.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of San Pasqual
properties.label: San Pasqual
properties.description: Californio lancers under Andrés Pico defeated Kearny's exhausted dragoons in the San Pasqual Valley, killing about 20 Americans. Kearny's force was besieged on a hill until relieved by sailors and marines from San Diego.
properties.modern_place: San Pasqual Battlefield State Historic Park

sources.citation: Dwight L. Clarke, Stephen Watts Kearny: Soldier of the West (University of Oklahoma Press, 1961).
K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).

properties.title: Treaty of Cahuenga
properties.label: Cahuenga
properties.description: After US forces under Stockton and Kearny won the skirmishes at the San Gabriel River and La Mesa (8–9 January) and reoccupied Los Angeles, Andrés Pico surrendered the Californio forces to Frémont at Campo de Cahuenga, ending the fighting in Alta California.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Dwight L. Clarke, Stephen Watts Kearny: Soldier of the West (University of Oklahoma Press, 1961).

properties.title: Doniphan's expedition to Chihuahua
properties.label: Doniphan 1846–47
properties.description: Alexander Doniphan's regiment of Missouri volunteers marched south from New Mexico down the Jornada del Muerto, won a skirmish at El Brazito on Christmas Day 1846, occupied El Paso del Norte, defeated a Mexican force at the Sacramento River and occupied Chihuahua City. It then marched east via Parras to join Taylor's army near Saltillo.
properties.note: Main stops only; the section from Chihuahua to Parras is schematic.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of the Sacramento River
properties.label: Sacramento
properties.description: Doniphan's Missourians defeated the larger but poorly armed Chihuahuan defenders at their fortified position on the Sacramento River north of Chihuahua City, and entered the city on 1 March.
properties.note: The battlefield lies roughly 25 km north of Chihuahua City; the point is approximate.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).

properties.title: Scott's campaign from Veracruz to Mexico City
properties.label: Scott 1847
properties.description: Winfield Scott landed near Veracruz, took the city after a siege and bombardment, and followed the old royal road up through Xalapa and Perote to Puebla, roughly retracing Cortés's route. Rather than attack the fortified eastern approach to Mexico City at El Peñón, he swung south around Lake Chalco and Xochimilco and fought his way in from the southwest.
properties.note: Main stops only. The army paused at Puebla from May to August 1847; the route around the southern lakes follows Bauer.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Siege of Veracruz
properties.label: Veracruz 1847
properties.description: Scott landed some 10,000 men on the beach at Collado south of the city in the largest US amphibious landing before the Second World War, then bombarded Veracruz into surrender. The city capitulated on 27 March and was occupied on the 29th; civilian casualties from the bombardment were heavy.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 10) gives 26 March for the surrender of the garrison.

properties.title: Battle of Cerro Gordo
properties.label: Cerro Gordo
properties.description: Santa Anna blocked the national road where it climbs out of the coastal lowlands, but US engineers (including Robert E. Lee) found a path around his left flank, and the Mexican army was routed. The way to Xalapa and the highlands lay open.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of Contreras (Padierna)
properties.label: Padierna
properties.description: US troops crossed the lava field of the Pedregal and, attacking at dawn from the rear, routed Gabriel Valencia's division at its camp near Padierna and San Jerónimo, which Santa Anna had failed to reinforce.
properties.modern_place: San Jerónimo Aculco, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of Churubusco
properties.label: Churubusco
properties.description: The same afternoon, the Franciscan convent of Churubusco and its bridgehead were defended by Mexican national guards and the San Patricio battalion, largely Irish immigrants and many of them deserters from the US army, who fought until their ammunition ran out. Captured San Patricios were hanged in September. A short armistice followed.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Battle of Molino del Rey
properties.label: Molino del Rey
properties.description: Believing a cannon foundry operated in the mill buildings west of Chapultepec, Scott attacked them. The US took the position at a heavy cost and found no foundry.
properties.note: The mills stood at the western foot of Chapultepec hill, near the present Los Pinos.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Storming of Chapultepec
properties.label: Chapultepec
properties.description: US troops stormed the hilltop castle that housed the Military College. Among its defenders were cadets later honoured as the Niños Héroes. The attackers then pushed along the causeways to the Belén and San Cosme gates of the city.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: US Army occupies Mexico City
properties.label: Mexico City occupied
properties.description: Santa Anna withdrew his army in the night and Scott's troops entered the capital and raised the US flag over the National Palace. Residents fought the occupiers in the streets for several days. The occupation lasted until June 1848.

sources.citation: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (Macmillan, 1974; repr. University of Nebraska Press, 1992).
Peter Guardino, The Dead March: A History of the Mexican-American War (Harvard University Press, 2017).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo signed
properties.label: Treaty signed
properties.description: Nicholas Trist, who had been recalled by Polk but stayed to negotiate, signed the peace treaty with Mexican commissioners at the town of Guadalupe Hidalgo beside the shrine of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
properties.modern_place: Basílica de Guadalupe, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Treaty of Peace, Friendship, Limits, and Settlement (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo), signed 2 Feb 1848, art. V. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Treaty ratified at Querétaro
properties.label: Querétaro 1848
properties.description: With Mexico City occupied, the Mexican government and Congress sat at Querétaro, where Congress approved the treaty against strong opposition and ratifications were exchanged with the US commissioners. US troops left Mexico City in June.

sources.citation: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), art. XXIII on ratification. Text: Avalon Project, Yale Law School.
Timothy J. Henderson, A Glorious Defeat: Mexico and Its War with the United States (Hill and Wang, 2007).
Josefina Zoraida Vázquez, "Los primeros tropiezos", in Historia general de México, versión 2000 (El Colegio de México, 2000).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Sierra Gorda rebellion (1847–1849)
properties.label: Sierra Gorda rebellion
properties.description: In the Sierra Gorda, the mountains where Guanajuato, Querétaro and San Luis Potosí meet, villagers resisted forced recruitment for the war with the United States, and deserters returning to Xichú in August 1847 began a revolt that spread across the sierra under Eleuterio Quiroz. In March 1849 his "Army Regenerator of the Sierra Gorda" proclaimed a plan at Rioverde demanding a fairer distribution of land, moderate rents for tenants and the conversion of the larger haciendas into villages. Government troops crushed the movement later that year. Gillingham notes that peasants in the Huasteca and Morelos likewise used the war to fight the government and the landowners rather than the invaders.
properties.note: Marked at Xichú, Guanajuato, where the revolt began; it ranged across the sierra to Rioverde and Santa María del Río in San Luis Potosí. The peasant risings of the Huasteca that Gillingham mentions, studied by Ducey, are not mapped separately.

sources.citation: Ulises Ramírez Casas, "'Mientras los generales duermen': Desobediencia militar y rebelión en Sierra Gorda durante el conflicto bélico entre México y los Estados Unidos, 1846-1849," Estudios de Historia Moderna y Contemporánea de México 60 (2020): 19–49.

Eleuterio Quiroz and Valentín Camargo, "Plan político y eminentemente social, proclamado en Río Verde por el Ejército Regenerador de la Sierra Gorda," 13 March 1849 (transcription, Historia Mexicana de los Planes e Insurrecciones, UNAM).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Republic of the Rio Grande
properties.label: Republic of the Rio Grande
properties.description: Federalists in Tamaulipas, Nuevo León and Coahuila, opposed to the centralist government, declared a separate republic based along the lower Rio Grande around Laredo and Guerrero. Defeated by centralist forces, its leaders submitted by November 1840. It shows how far the northeast's grievances ran beyond Texas.
properties.note: Marked at Laredo, where independence was proclaimed on 17 January 1840; the seat of government moved to Guerrero and later into Texas. It ended with Antonio Canales's capitulation at Camargo in November 1840.

sources.citation: Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Republic of the Rio Grande".
Josefina Zoraida Vázquez, "Los primeros tropiezos", in Historia general de México, versión 2000 (El Colegio de México, 2000).

properties.title: Texan Santa Fe Expedition captured
properties.label: Texan Santa Fe Expedition
properties.description: President Mirabeau Lamar sent an armed trading expedition from Austin to assert the Texas claim to the upper Rio Grande and draw Santa Fe's trade to Texas. Exhausted after crossing the plains, its advance party surrendered to Governor Armijo's forces near Anton Chico and the main body near present-day Tucumcari; the prisoners were marched to Mexico, an episode that hardened opinion on both sides.
properties.note: The expedition surrendered in groups in September and October 1841 in eastern New Mexico; the point marks Anton Chico.

sources.citation: Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association), "Texan Santa Fe Expedition".
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).

properties.title: Commodore Jones seizes Monterey by mistake (1842)
properties.label: Jones at Monterey
properties.description: Believing that war had broken out and that Britain was about to take California, Commodore Thomas ap Catesby Jones of the US Pacific Squadron sailed into Monterey, the capital of Alta California, and landed sailors and marines; the small garrison surrendered without a fight and the US flag was raised over the castillo. Two days later, having learned from American newspapers that there was no war, he hauled it down, saluted the Mexican flag and apologised. Gillingham reads the episode as a sign of the attitudes that led to war four years later, when Sloat landed at the same port.
properties.note: Marked at the Presidio of Monterey, the site of the old castillo. Gillingham (ch. 10) gives September 1842 and eight hundred men; the dates here follow the local and US Navy accounts.

sources.citation: Gene A. Smith, Thomas ap Catesby Jones: Commodore of Manifest Destiny (Naval Institute Press, 2000).
Mayo Hayes O'Donnell, "The Commodore Who Dreamed Up a War," Peninsula Diary, 23 February 1951 (Monterey History and Art Association).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Comanche raiding into northern Mexico
properties.label: Comanche war trail
properties.description: From the 1830s Comanche and Kiowa war parties rode south each autumn from the southern plains, crossed the Rio Grande around the Big Bend and raided as deep as Durango, Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí, killing and capturing thousands and driving off livestock; in December 1840 some four hundred riders reached San Luis Potosí and attacked Saltillo on the way back. The raids emptied much of the north of settlers and resources before the US invasion, and the US promise to stop them (art. XI of Guadalupe Hidalgo) was later cancelled by the Gadsden Treaty.
properties.note: One representative corridor (the "Great Comanche War Trail" via Comanche Springs and the Big Bend); raids also crossed the lower Rio Grande into Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, and Apache raiding affected Sonora and Chihuahua.

sources.citation: Brian DeLay, War of a Thousand Deserts: Indian Raids and the U.S.–Mexican War (Yale University Press, 2008).
David J. Weber, The Mexican Frontier, 1821–1846: The American Southwest under Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 1982).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: William Walker's filibuster in Baja California
properties.label: Walker filibuster
properties.description: The American adventurer William Walker seized La Paz with a small private army and proclaimed a "Republic of Lower California", then moved to Ensenada, where he proclaimed a "Republic of Sonora", before Mexican resistance and lack of supplies forced him back across the border. It ran alongside the Gadsden negotiations and fed Mexican fears of further US expansion.
properties.note: Marked at La Paz, where the filibusters landed.

sources.citation: Joseph A. Stout Jr., Schemers & Dreamers: Filibustering in Mexico, 1848–1921 (TCU Press, 2002).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Raousset-Boulbon defeated at Guaymas
properties.label: Guaymas 1854
properties.description: The French adventurer Gaston de Raousset-Boulbon, who had earlier tried to seize Sonora's mines, landed at Guaymas with a filibustering force and was defeated by the Mexican garrison under José María Yáñez; he was executed in August. Sonora's exposure to such schemes was another sign of how weakly the national government held the northwest.

sources.citation: Rufus Kay Wyllys, The French in Sonora (1850–1854): The Story of French Adventurers from California into Mexico (University of California Press, 1932).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
